title: Blessings on the Prophet ﷺ
hook: Allah and His angels send blessings on the Prophet, so do the same (33:56)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Umm Salamah, and a verse that names women and men, pair after pair. Your line was both, equally.

Look at any page of a Muslim book, a sermon transcript, a social media post about the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. After his name, there's a small curl of Arabic calligraphy, or four letters in brackets, or the words peace be upon him. It can start to feel like punctuation. But it isn't a habit someone invented to be polite. It comes from one verse in Al-Ahzab, a verse that says who does it first, before anyone on earth.
screen: `ONE VERSE SAYS WHO DOES IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Verse fifty-six. Pickthall: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." Look at the order. First Allah. Then the angels. Only then the believers, asked to join something already happening. The Arabic word is salat, the same word as the daily prayer. Bukhari records an early explanation from Abu al-'Aliya: Allah's salat is His praise of the Prophet before the angels, and the angels' salat is their prayer for him. When believers send it, it's a request: O Allah, bless him. Blessings like these are called salawat, and a common form begins Allahumma salli, O Allah, send blessings. The small curl in print stands for sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam: may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Many Muslims say it aloud or write it when his name comes up. Many count them, too, because a hadith in Sahih Muslim says that whoever sends one blessing on the Prophet, Allah sends ten blessings on that person. One out, ten back. Near the end of the daily prayer, Muslims recite a longer salawat, often called the Abrahamic blessing, asking that Muhammad and his family be blessed as Ibrahim and his family were blessed. Sunni and Shia Muslims both include the Prophet's family in it; the exact wording varies by school. So the little curl is the end of a long chain: Allah, the angels, and then anyone who reads the name and stops for one breath.
screen: `ALLAH, THEN THE ANGELS, THEN THE BELIEVERS.`

segments.voice: If you're Muslim, or want to try, say the short form ten times, quietly, counting on your fingers: Allahumma salli 'ala Muhammad, O Allah, send blessings on Muhammad. If that isn't your practice, sit with the verse's picture instead: a blessing already moving, from Allah, through the angels, and an invitation to join in. Either way, end in silence.
Salawat. Blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, what Allah and the angels send first, and what believers ask for, one blessing out and ten returned. Today's word.
Your line: blessings on him. One verse, and a long chain behind the little curl. That's the last of Al-Ahzab.

chat.says: Why do Muslims write a little symbol after the Prophet's name?
options: It's a short blessing on him; the Qur'an says Allah and the angels bless him first.
It's a mark old scribes added to show the name is spelled correctly.
It's a polite habit, like a title, with no root in the Qur'an itself.
chat.meaning: Al-Ahzab 33:56 says Allah and His angels bless the Prophet, then asks believers to join in. The symbol stands for that blessing.

Abu al-'Aliya.meaning: an early scholar whose explanation Bukhari records

Ibrahim.meaning: Abraham, the prophet named in the Abrahamic blessing
